title: Preparing to Build: Solomon and Hiram of Tyre
summary: Solomon resolves to build a house for the LORD's Name and a palace for himself, and he organizes a vast labor force. He writes to Hiram king of Tyre asking for timber from Lebanon and a master craftsman, explaining that no house can contain God. Hiram replies with praise for Israel's God, sends the skilled Huram-abi, and agrees to float the logs to Joppa in exchange for grain, wine, and oil.
story: The gift of wisdom in chapter 1 now turns into action. The temple David planned and provided for (1 Chronicles 22 to 29) moves from blueprint to building site. This chapter is the preparation: labor, materials, and expertise. The Chronicler makes the preparation itself an occasion for theology, because Solomon's letter to Hiram explains what the temple is for and what it cannot be. Chapters 3 and 4 will describe the construction, and chapters 5 to 7 its dedication.
historical:
Tyre was the leading Phoenician city, built on an island off the coast of what is now Lebanon, and the center of a trading network that reached across the Mediterranean. Its king Hiram (Hebrew Huram in Chronicles) had supplied cedar for David's palace (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Chronicles 14:1). The parallel account in 1 Kings 5 describes the same agreement, with some differences in detail: in Kings, Solomon pays Hiram's household annually in wheat and pressed oil, while here the payment is wheat, barley, wine, and oil for the woodcutters. The two may describe different parts of the arrangement.

The cedar forests of Lebanon were prized across the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian and Egyptian rulers boasted of bringing cedar from Lebanon for their palaces and temples. Logs were lashed into rafts, floated down the coast, and landed at Joppa (modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv), the nearest port to Jerusalem, then hauled some thirty-five miles (about fifty-five kilometers) inland and uphill. Note that English Bibles number this chapter differently from the Hebrew: English 2:1 is Hebrew 1:18, and English 2:2-18 is Hebrew 2:1-17.
cultural:
Solomon's letter describes the daily worship that the temple would house: fragrant incense, the showbread (twelve loaves displayed before God and renewed each Sabbath), burnt offerings every morning and evening, and the special sacrifices of Sabbaths, new moons, and annual feasts (verse 4). This is the worship prescribed in the law of Moses, and for the Chronicler's readers, who had the second temple and its daily rhythm, it was their own worship.

The Phoenicians were famous for fine craftsmanship and for purple dye, produced at great cost from murex sea snails, which made purple the color of royalty. The purple, crimson, and blue yarns in verses 7 and 14 were the colors of the tabernacle curtains in Exodus. Huram-abi's mother was from the tribe of Dan and his father from Tyre, so he stood between the two peoples. The labor force of verses 17 and 18 was drawn from the non-Israelite peoples living in the land, the remnants of the Canaanite population, whom ancient kings routinely conscripted for state building projects.
literary: The chapter is framed by matching notices about the labor force (verses 2 and 17-18), which give the same numbers: 70,000 porters, 80,000 stonecutters, and 3,600 supervisors. Between them sit two letters, Solomon's request (3 to 10) and Hiram's reply (11 to 16). Solomon's letter includes a short theological reflection: the house will be great because God is great, yet not even the highest heavens can contain him (verses 5-6). Hiram's reply, from a foreign king, praises the LORD as maker of heaven and earth and calls Solomon a wise son. The Chronicler also shapes Huram-abi as a second Oholiab, the Danite craftsman who worked with Bezalel on the tabernacle (Exodus 31:6), so that the temple's builders echo the tabernacle's.

outline.t: Solomon's purpose and his labor force
Hiram's reply and the gift of Huram-abi
The census of foreigners and the workforce

doctrines.note: Solomon confesses that “the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him” (verse 6). The temple is not a box for God but a place where people may meet him and offer worship. God's greatness exceeds anything built for him.

A foreign king blesses “the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth” (verse 12), and foreign skill and timber go into God's house. Already the nations are drawn into Israel's worship, a thread the Bible follows to its end.

The temple's purpose is defined by worship: incense, bread, and sacrifice, morning and evening, Sabbath and feast. It is ordained “for Israel forever” (verse 4). The building exists for the service of a holy God.

words.note: Chakham, wise or skilled. It appears six times in this chapter, used both of Solomon (“a wise son”) and of the craftsmen who work metal and cloth. In Hebrew wisdom includes technical skill. The same quality that lets Solomon govern lets Huram-abi engrave gold; both are gifts for building God's house.

Shamayim, heavens or sky. Solomon uses it in the phrase “the heavens, even the highest heavens”, literally the heavens and the heavens of heavens, a Hebrew way of saying the uttermost heights. Even they cannot hold God, so how much less a building.

Ger, sojourner or resident foreigner. Verse 17 counts the foreigners living in Israel and puts them to work. The law of Moses commanded Israel to love the sojourner and treat him fairly, because Israel had been sojourners in Egypt; this verse shows the other side, their use as state labor.

Ahavah, love. Hiram's letter says the LORD made Solomon king because he “loves His people” (verse 11). Israel's king is God's gift to his people, and the reason for the gift is God's love, spoken here by an outsider.

christ: Solomon's question, how can anyone build a house for the God whom the heavens cannot contain, runs through the whole Bible. Solomon will ask it again in his dedication prayer (6:18), and Stephen quotes Isaiah's version of it in Acts 7:48-50 to show that God does not live in houses made by hands. The New Testament's answer is the incarnation: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and Jesus called his own body the temple (John 2:21). The involvement of a foreign king and foreign craftsmen in the building also anticipates the gospel's reach. Isaiah pictured the wealth of the nations and the glory of Lebanon coming to beautify God's sanctuary (Isaiah 60), and Paul describes Gentile believers being built together with Jews into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:19-22). These are thematic connections; the chapter itself is about timber and craftsmen.

hard.q: Were Solomon's builders forced labor, and does the Bible approve of it?
hard.a:
Verses 17 and 18 describe Solomon counting the foreigners in the land and assigning them as porters and stonecutters. First Kings 9:20-22 and 2 Chronicles 8:7-9 say these were descendants of the Canaanite peoples and that Israelites were not made slaves. Yet 1 Kings 5:13-14 also describes a levy of 30,000 Israelites sent to Lebanon in shifts, and 1 Kings 12 shows that Solomon's heavy yoke of labor was the grievance that split the kingdom after his death. So the Bible itself records the burden and its cost.

Interpreters generally note that corvée (compulsory state labor) was standard in the ancient world and that the text reports it rather than commends it. The law of Moses repeatedly calls Israel to remember its own slavery in Egypt and to treat foreigners justly, and the prophets later condemned kings who built with unpaid labor (Jeremiah 22:13). The Chronicler, focused on the temple, does not pause to criticize, but the wider biblical story does, and 2 Chronicles 10 will show the price.

questions: Solomon wanted to build something great for God while admitting that no building could contain him. How do you hold together giving your best to God and knowing he doesn't need it?
A foreign king praised Israel's God and helped build his house. Where have you seen people outside the church recognize something true about God?
Huram-abi's craft skill is called wisdom. What skills do you have that could be offered to God as a form of wisdom?
